# Copilot Instructions

## Project Overview
- A physically-based ray tracer with parallel CPU and GPU (OptiX) implementations, built up from "Ray Tracing in One Weekend"/"The Next Week"/"The Rest of Your Life" into a pbrt-v4-style feature set: 175 built-in scenes (id = category letter + number, e.g. `A1`, `B10`, `G25` — see `src/shared/scene_descriptor.h`'s `SceneCategories`, not a flat integer), a wide material/BxDF library, multiple light and camera types, real triangle-mesh + texture support, BVH acceleration, volumetrics, and an SPPM (photon-mapping) integrator alongside standard path tracing. See README.md for the full feature list and Known Limitations for what's still incomplete (GPU SPPM handles only spheres, quads, area lights, a uniform sky and textured diffuse surfaces and rejects anything else; BDPT/MLT are CPU-only and support neither portal lights nor camera media; scene B11's hair uses a shading-normal proxy rather than real fiber geometry, unlike scene F4's real curve geometry; etc.) — don't assume everything mentioned in code comments is fully wired up; check.
- Active production code lives in `src/TheRestOfYourLife/` (CPU scenes/materials/lights) and `src/shared/` (CPU+GPU shared headers: BxDFs, cameras, lights, sampling — many are `CPU_GPU`-tagged templates compiled by both the host compiler and nvcc).
- **The unified launcher entry point is `launcher/main.cpp`**, not a root-level `main.cpp` — an earlier root-level `main.cpp` was the one that got deleted; the file now lives alongside `launcher/launcher.vcxproj`, which references it as plain `main.cpp` (its own directory), not `..\main.cpp`. GPU is the default render mode (`--gpu`); `--cpu` and `--sppm` are opt-in flags.
- The CPU renderer is a static library project named `cpu_renderer` (formerly `raytracing_book`). It builds `cpu_renderer.lib`, linked into the launcher via a ProjectReference, called in-process through `cpu_render_main()` (`cpu_renderer/cpu_interface.h`).
- The GPU renderer uses OptiX 9.1 and is built as a static library project named `optix_renderer`, building `optix_renderer.lib`, called in-process through `optix_render_main()` (`gpu/optix/optix_interface.h`). Three GPU backends exist: the default recursive mega-kernel (`gpu/optix/optix_programs.cu`), an opt-in wavefront/queue-based path tracer (`gpu/optix/wavefront_*`, enabled via the `--wavefront` CLI flag), and GPU SPPM (`gpu/optix/sppm_*`, `--sppm --gpu`, sphere/quad scenes only). macOS has a separate Metal backend in `gpu/metal/` (`-DRT_BUILD_METAL=ON`).
- Films (cartoons and film files, `--video-preset`, `scripts/anim/film.py`) live in `src/shared/cartoon/` and `launcher/`; each frame is written as a `.pbrt` file and rendered by a child run of the launcher. `docs/VIDEO_GENERATION.md` is the reference.
- Build environment: CUDA compilation requires Visual Studio Developer Command Prompt/PowerShell (vcvars64.bat). Regular PowerShell causes nvcc/cudafe++ access violations.
- **GPU hardware**: developed against an RTX 5080 (Blackwell, SM 12.0), driver 595.79+, OptiX 9.1, CUDA 13.2+.

## Build System Gotcha: PTX/obj staleness across output directories
- The optix_renderer project's custom MSBuild targets copy freshly-built PTX (`optix_programs.ptx`, `wavefront_programs.ptx`, `sppm_programs.ptx`) to `RayTracer_Package/` automatically, but **not reliably to `bin/Release/` or `x64/Release/`** (the test binary's own output directories) — this has caused real, reproducible-looking GPU test failures ("invalid program counter" CUDA errors) that were actually just stale PTX, not code bugs. If you touch any header shared between host code and device `.cu` files (e.g. a struct in `optix_types.h`), **touch all the `.cu` files** (`optix_programs.cu`, `wavefront_*.cu`, `sppm_*.cu`) to force MSBuild to recompile their PTX/obj, then verify with `md5sum` that `gpu/optix/*.ptx`, `bin/Release/*.ptx`, `x64/Release/*.ptx`, and `RayTracer_Package/*.ptx` all match before trusting a GPU test run.
- Even after confirming PTX consistency, the full test suite (all in one process) shows genuine non-deterministic GPU-resource-pressure flakiness under `--gtest_shuffle` with different seeds — a handful of GPU tests near the end of a long run can fail even when the code is correct. Don't chase this as a code bug without first re-running with shuffled order/seeds to check reproducibility. For everyday iteration use `scripts\run_tests_parallel.ps1 -Tier Fast` (the cheap, GPU-free tests in parallel shards, about 75 s); `-Tier Split` runs the whole suite (Fast, then Render and Slow) — see `tests/TESTING_GUIDE.md`. Run the Render/Slow tiers too when rendering code changed.

## Qt GUI Application
- The Qt-based GUI is located in `qt_gui/` and built using Qt 6.11.1 with the MSVC 2022 64-bit kit.
- The GUI executable is `RayTracerGUI.exe` and is deployed to the `RayTracer_Package/` directory.
- The GUI spawns the console launcher `ray_tracer.exe` as a subprocess to perform rendering. Scene metadata (description, GPU compatibility, perf hint) is loaded live from a separate `scene_metadata.dll` (built from `scene_metadata.vcxproj`), not hardcoded in the GUI; the GUI's film table comes from the same DLL — **this DLL must be rebuilt (and installed beside `ray_tracer.exe`) whenever `scene_registry.h` or the films change**, or the GUI will show a stale scene or film list. `RayTracerGUI.exe` holds a lock on this DLL while running, so it needs to be closed before rebuilding.
- **Deployment**: MSBuild automatically deploys `ray_tracer.exe` and the OptiX PTX files to `RayTracer_Package/` via post-build events when you build the launcher or optix_renderer projects. No manual copying needed for those two, but see the PTX staleness gotcha above for `bin/`/`x64/` test-binary directories.
- **Verification**: Run `.\scripts\deploy_launcher.ps1` to verify deployment succeeded after building.
- **Qt dependencies**: Run `windeployqt.exe RayTracerGUI.exe --no-translations` in the `RayTracer_Package` directory to deploy Qt6 DLLs if missing.

## Rendering Guidelines
- Scenes are `.pbrt` files in `pbrt_scenes/`. The 175 built-in ones have a row in `src/TheRestOfYourLife/scene_registry_data.h` (name, category, description, measured performance), a durable name in `src/shared/scene_slugs.h`, and a technique note in `qt_gui/scene_technique_notes.h`; a test scene or a scene of your own needs only header tags (`# @rt-category`, `# @rt-description`, ...). The CPU and GPU builders read the same file, so there is no second scene description to keep in sync. See `docs/SCENE_SELECTION.md`.
- Both GPU backends now do real importance sampling (NEE + MIS), matching the CPU renderer's approach — the recursive backend shares CPU's own `PowerHeuristic()` (`src/shared/math_utils.h`) via `shade_material()` (`gpu/optix/optix_device_helpers.h`); the wavefront backend has its own independent `wf_mis()` (`gpu/optix/wavefront_device_helpers.h`), used from `wavefront_kernels_materials.cu`'s `evaluate_materials()`. Older code/comments may still say the GPU "requires ~100x more samples" or "uses naive path tracing" from an earlier, pre-MIS GPU implementation — that claim is stale; don't trust it without checking current `shade_material()`/`evaluate_materials()` first.
- Set the ray-origin offset appropriately (historically 0.01f for 555-unit Cornell box scenes) to prevent self-intersection; use a minimum t-value of 0.001f for sphere intersections instead of 0.0f.
- Mesh/environment scenes (category **G** Models and **H** Large Scenes - e.g. `G1`-`G25`+, `H1`+) load external `.obj` files from `models/`, searched via a climbing relative-path convention (tries `models/`, `../models/`, `../../models/`, ... up to 5-6 levels) so a single asset copy works regardless of the render's current working directory (`RayTracer_Package/`, `bin/Release/`, a test binary's own cwd, ...). `models/` holds the statue meshes as ordinary files (it is no longer in Git LFS); the largest scenes (Sponza, Bistro, Rungholt, San Miguel, ...) are not in the repository at all, and the GUI's "Download missing files" fetches them into a per-user assets folder the renderer also searches (`docs/SCENE_SELECTION.md`, "Scenes that need files").

## File Handling Guidelines
- Visual Studio holds exclusive write locks on open .cpp files. An editor tool that writes to Visual Studio's in-memory buffer (visible in the editor) does NOT flush to disk while Visual Studio has the file open.
- PowerShell's `Set-Content` will fail with "file being used by another process."
- Workaround: Create a new file instead of editing a file that is currently open in the IDE, or verify on-disk content before trusting tool-view edits.
- **Line endings**: most C++ sources are CRLF, but a growing number have been converted to LF (see the line-endings commits in `.git-blame-ignore-revs`), and `*.sh` is always LF. Keep each file's own line endings; check a file for mixed endings after an edit with `perl -ne 'print if /\r(?!\n)|(?<!\r)\n/' <file> | wc -l` (0 for a CRLF file). Edit with an editor or edit tool, not shell heredocs that carry backslash escapes: the shell layer has corrupted `\n` and stray carriage returns that way (one in a comment of `film_file.h` broke every non-MSVC build).

## Terminal Guidelines
- Always read terminal output promptly rather than waiting long durations for terminal commands.
